subject: Computer Science
topic: Search traces, invariants and meaningful complexity claims
scope: Untiered A-Level lesson on linear, binary and binary-search-tree search. Includes executable JavaScript examples and traces, not completion of the programming project or every algorithm in 4.3. Original teaching and practice, not official examination material. Practice rubrics are for self-review. This topic does not establish whole-course coverage, independent subject review or publication approval.
prerequisites: Understand ascending order and powers of two.
objectives: Explain binary search’s precondition and shrinking interval.
Qualify complexity claims by data structure and case.

notes.heading: Linear search and its contract
paragraphs: A search procedure needs a defined result for both success and failure. This JavaScript implementation returns the first matching zero-based index or -1: function linearSearch(a, target) { for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] === target) return i; } return -1; }. It works on unsorted arrays. In the worst case it checks every element, giving O(n) time; finding the first element is a best case requiring constant time. Empty input returns -1 without accessing an element.

notes.heading: Binary search and what remains possible
paragraphs: For an ascending sorted array, use this implementation: function binarySearch(a, target) { let low = 0; let high = a.length - 1; while (low <= high) { const mid = Math.floor((low + high) / 2); if (a[mid] === target) return mid; if (a[mid] < target) low = mid + 1; else high = mid - 1; } return -1; }. At each iteration any possible match remains inside the inclusive interval from low to high. Ordering justifies discarding the other half. The +1 or -1 excludes the inspected midpoint and ensures progress; without it, a small interval can repeat forever.

notes.heading: Tracing and growth rates
paragraphs: Trace low, high, mid and the inspected value on every iteration. In [3,7,12,18,24,31,40], searching for 31 checks 18 and then 31, returning index 5. Searching for 25 checks 18,31,24 and then terminates with an empty interval. Halving repeatedly gives logarithmic worst-case growth, O(log n). This describes growth of work, not an exact duration in seconds. A single lookup in unsorted data may not justify sorting first; sorting cost and how often searches repeat affect the decision.

notes.heading: Binary search trees need a shape assumption
paragraphs: A binary search tree places smaller keys in a node’s left subtree and larger keys in the right, under a stated duplicate policy. Search follows one branch after each comparison. Time depends on height: a balanced tree has height proportional to log n, while inserting already sorted keys into an ordinary unbalanced tree can produce a chain of height proportional to n. Therefore the useful O(log n) claim requires an appropriate shape or balancing assumption. A tree is not guaranteed fast merely because each node has at most two children.

steps: Start low=0, high=4, mid=2, value=8, so high=1.
mid=0 gives 2, so low=1; mid=1 gives 5.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare searching an ordinary BST made by inserting 1,2,3,4 in that order with a balanced tree.
steps: Each new larger key follows the right branch.
The height, rather than the label binary, determines the worst-case search length.
workedExamples.answer: The ordinary insertion creates a rightward chain; searching for 4 visits all four nodes.

misconceptions.claim: Binary search works on any array.
misconceptions.correction: Its discard step depends on sorted order.

misconceptions.claim: Every binary search tree guarantees logarithmic search.
misconceptions.correction: An unbalanced tree can become a linear chain.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] For the supplied linearSearch, what is returned for [4,9,4] with target 4, and for [] with target 4?
solution: The empty array executes no loop iterations.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Trace the supplied binarySearch on [1,4,9,16,25,36,49] for target 36. Give inspected values and returned index.
solution: Initial midpoint index 3 has value 16, so low=4.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Trace the same seven-item array for target 20. Give the inspected values and the final low/high pair.
solution: After 16, search indices 4 to 6; after 36, high=4.
At index 4, 25 is too large, so high=3 and the interval is empty.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Why can replacing low = mid + 1 with low = mid prevent termination?
questions.answer: When low equals mid and the target is greater, the same interval and midpoint can repeat.
solution: Consider a one-element interval with a larger absent target.
The bound must move beyond the already-tested element.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Why might linear search be sensible for one lookup in an unsorted small array despite binary search’s lower asymptotic search cost?
questions.answer: Binary search requires sorting or already ordered data; preparation and constants can outweigh one lookup’s savings.
solution: Distinguish growth rate from guaranteed elapsed-time superiority.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] An ordinary BST receives distinct keys 10,20,30,40,50 in order. Explain its worst-case search growth.
questions.answer: It becomes a rightward chain; worst-case search is O(n).
solution: Each insertion goes right of all earlier keys.
Height grows with item count rather than logarithmically.

revisionGuide.summary: Correctness needs a contract and progress; performance needs a case and structural assumptions. Trace the actual implementation before naming a complexity class.
keyIdeas: What does -1 mean in these implementations? No matching array index was found.
What precondition does binary search need? Ascending sorted input for this implementation.
Why update low to mid + 1? The midpoint has been checked and must be excluded to ensure progress.
What is worst-case linear-search time? O(n).
What governs BST search cost? Tree height; balance gives logarithmic height.
